title: Integrated exposome profiling to identify environmental risk factors of metabolic disease in mid- and late-life
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because given the widespread exposure to metabolism
disrupting chemicals and the burden of T2D and MetS in the United States and globally, the public health
impact would be substantial if these modifiable exposures are reduced. The findings of this project will highlight
the clinical and public health utility of exposome for risk assessment, prevention, and precision health which
will effectively reduce metabolic disease risk.

title: Host and viral determinants of hepatitis B virus transcription
text:
Chronic viral infections are notoriously challenging to cure, and many result in long-term health complications
such as cancer due to sustained inflammation and cellular damage. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) can establish a
chronic infection in the liver, and viral persistence is achieved through the establishment of a stable episomal
DNA genome that serves as the template for transcription of all viral RNAs. A greater understanding of the host
factors and viral determinants of HBV transcription will have significant implications for studies of HBV infection
and pathogenesis, transcription of other virus- or host-derived episomal DNAs, and could ultimately lead to the
development of new curative treatments for HBV.

title: Novel methods to detect and interpret splicing quantitative trait loci - Renewal
text:
This project will reveal mechanistic links between human genetic variants, changes in the regulation of our genes,
and disease. These findings will contribute to both the interpretation of variations in our genome and the
prediction of outcomes for such variations, both with respect to disease and to therapeutic efficacy.

title: Role for ICP0 and UL55/UL13/Us10 in protein degradation in neurons and reactivation of HSV from latent infection
text:
Herpes simplex viruses persists for life in neurons as a latent infection and can reactivate to cause
disease. The aims of this study are to identify host proteins that are targeted for degradation following
infection and the contribution of viral proteins in both degradation and reactivation. Our long-term goals
are to understand the consequence of HSV persistent neuronal infection and identify new targets for
therapeutics that prevent reactivation of HSV.

title: University of Michigan Vision Research Center
text:
The University of Michigan Vision Research Center provides state-of-the-art equipment and technical
expertise and service for scientists at the University of Michigan to advance research programs into
understanding the visual system and to develop novel therapies to treat blinding eye disease and improve
the visual health of the country.

title: SPOT-IT: Sepsis Prediction in Oncology Through Implementation Science and Technology
text:
Because hospitalized patients with cancer face unacceptable morbidity and mortality from sepsis (a life-
threatening dysregulated response to infection), there is urgent need for interventions to identify oncologic
sepsis early and enable timelier appropriate treatments. However, incumbent electronic health record-based
sepsis prediction tools – linked to improved mortality in other populations – have failed to deliver on their
promise in oncology because of design and implementation limitations. This project aims to advance the
simultaneous and iterative development of a machine learning tool to predict oncologic sepsis alongside the
user-centered design of implementation strategies to improve sepsis care and outcomes for hospitalized
patients with cancer.

title: Enhancing Lamellar Body Function via LRRK2 Inhibition to Reduce Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) Severity
text:
Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) affects preterm infants due to insufficient surfactant production, and while
current therapies (exogenous surfactant replacement and antenatal corticosteroids) enhance endogenous
surfactant production, they carry significant short- and long-term risks. This study will test whether LRRK2
inhibition enhances the autophagy-driven lamellar body biogenesis pathway to increase surfactant reserve
capacity by defining the mechanism in human lung organoids, determining efficacy in preterm lambs, and
establishing neonatal safety. If successful, this research will validate LRRK2 inhibition as a novel
pharmacological therapy to stimulate endogenous surfactant production without steroid-associated toxicity and
potentially transform outcomes for premature infants.

title: Utilizing MRI and sensorimotor measures to phenotype adrenomyeloneuropathy progression.
text:
Adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN), the most common form of X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, is an untreatable
disorder that leads to significant disability for adult males and females (heterozygotes). The symptom profile and
progression rate are heterogeneous, and sensitive outcome measures and biomarkers remain elusive, which
has contributed to knowledge gaps and failure of trials. This project will apply machine learning tools to identify
AMN phenotypes using quantitative sensorimotor data and localize these phenotypes to MRI indices of
damage in spinal cord white matter tracts to elucidate pathological structure-function relationships.

title: Enabling Protein Sequencing Through Friction-Mediated Nanopore Transport
text:
This technology will open new markets and accelerate innovation across biomedical research, clinical
diagnostics, drug development, synthetic biology, biotechnology, and personalized medicine. By enabling direct,
high-resolution protein sequencing with modification-specific detail, it addresses longstanding unmet needs that
genomic methods alone cannot resolve. Its success will catalyze the rise of proteome-scale tools in single-cell
biology, real-time disease tracking, biologics manufacturing, and precision health, creating transformative
commercial opportunities akin to those once sparked by the genomics revolution.

title: Retrospective Magnetic Resonance Image Harmonization for Robust Federated Learning
text:
Machine learning algorithms can perform poorly when trying to analyze magnetic resonance imaging data
because their appearance is highly variable and often different from the data that was used to train the
algorithms. We will develop methods to make the algorithms more robust by training them with larger amounts
of data from multiple institutions while simultaneously reducing the variation in their appearance. We will
demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by building algorithms to automatically find lesions in magnetic
resonance brain images from people with multiple sclerosis.

title: Novel metrics of brain dynamics in Alzheimer’s disease
text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition and daily
functioning in older adults. This proposal seeks to better understand the association between alterations in
dynamic functional brain activity as it relates to biomarkers and decreasing cognition in individuals with mild
cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease, as well as cognitively intact seniors. This project will inform clinical
trials by predicting biomarker status based on dynamic functional connectivity in older adults with and without
cognitive impairment.

title: Gastrointestinal Insights into Anorexia Nervosa Treatment
text: This novel project aims to investigate the underexamined, biological mechanisms driving gastroparesis in chronic anorexia nervosa (AN), a severe condition characterized by high morbidity and limited treatment options. Gastroparesis, a condition where the stomach's ability to empty its contents is delayed, is highly prevalent in individuals with chronic AN and may play a key role in perpetuating the disorder. The slowing of gastric emptying contributes to a range of gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms, such as early satiety, nausea, and bloating, which research has shown can heighten fear of eating and reinforce food restriction behaviors. This creates a vicious cycle where AN cognitions and behaviors, along with physiological dysfunction, feed into one another, making it harder to treat the disorder effectively. However, to date, no study has thoroughly attempted to address how gastrointestinal dysfunction may play a role in the maintenance of chronic AN. By focusing on interactions between glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gut microbiota dysbiosis, and gastric emptying, we aim to explore how these factors contribute to the persistence of AN. Specifically, we hypothesize that slower gastric emptying correlates with increased selfreported AN symptoms, with gastroparesis partially mediating this relationship. Additionally, we will examine how GLP-1 responsiveness and gut microbial beta-diversity moderate the relationships between gastric emptying, gastroparesis, and AN behaviors. Data will be collected from participants on an inpatient eating disorder unit through laboratory assessments, including gastric emptying evaluations and GLP-1 response measurements, along with ecological momentary assessments (EMA) tracking symptoms over two weeks. A second fecal sample and clinical information collected one month post-discharge will assess changes in gut microbiota diversity and GI distress. By elucidating these mechanisms, this research has the potential to inform novel treatments (i.e., emerging pharmacological interventions such as GLP-1 antagonists) that reduce the chronicity of AN and address the "crisis in care" for individuals with this challenging disorder.

title: Animal Models & Phenotyping Core
text: PROJECT SUMMARY - ANIMAL MODELS & PHENOTYPING CORE The Animal Models and Phenotyping Core (AMPC) supports animal-based studies across the NORC theme of “Nutrition, Obesity and Metabolic Health through the Lifespan”. These services focus on two primary areas: 1) creating genetically modified animal models, and 2) providing state-of-the-art in vivo metabolic and behavioral phenotyping of rodent models. Over past funding cycles, the AMPC has been a key component of the overall mission of the Pennington-Louisiana NORC, enhancing and facilitating funded research while also stimulating new and innovative research related to nutrition and obesity. The AMPC is essential for a broad range of research within the NORC, supporting more than 38 NIDDK and other NIH grants in the past cycle while also interacting closely with the Administrative Core, Molecular Mechanisms Core (now the Bioinformatics and Molecular Mechanisms Core), and the Human Phenotyping Core to assure success in achieving the Specific Aims of each research project. This critical support will be sustained in the current cycle by: A) continuing to create genetically modified rodent models (mice and rats) that recapitulate human metabolic disease states; B) using state-of-the-art equipment and technology to conduct detailed in vivo metabolic and behavioral phenotyping, and; C) providing consultation related to rodent nutrition and obesity research, training in the use of experimental services, and pursuing new methods and experimental paradigms that anticipate the needs of NORC members and Pilot and Feasibility projects. Through these goals, the AMPC will directly support the use of animal models to better understand the pathophysiology of human metabolic disease states in a translational research approach while also facilitating cross-talk among scientists focused on nutrition and obesity research.

title: Light pipe microscope for ultra-large-scale cellular-resolution whole-neocortex two-photon calcium imaging of mammalian brains
text:
This project will develop a low-cost, scalable two-photon imaging platform, the Light Pipe Microscope (LPM),
that enables cellular-resolution imaging across most of the mammalian neocortex. The resulting technology will
enable new studies of brain-wide circuit dynamics, including how activity spreads through cortical networks
during learning, behavior, and neurological disorders. Such capabilities may accelerate the development of
treatments for diseases involving abnormal network activity, including epilepsy.

title: Discovery of novel tau proteoforms as biomarker candidates for AD and PSP
text:
Although the last five years have seen tremendous advancements in the use of tau biomarkers in blood, there
remains a need to discover new and improved markers that will better inform on risk of cognitive decline in
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) or aid in an earlier diagnosis of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) or other non-
AD tauopathies. Results from our innovative studies will provide additional evidence of tau proteoform
differences in the human brain between AD and PSP and explore how tau immunotherapy treatment
influences what forms are identified in blood. These studies will identify biomarker candidates for exploration
of clinical utility across primary tauopathies, and will have potential to inform on progression, enable earlier
diagnosis, and enable clinical trials at earlier stages.

title: Small molecule enhancers of tumor immunity targeting the LPA5 GPCR
text:
In an effort to overcome the ability of numerous cancers to evade the immune system, a drug
lead development campaign utilizing cutting-edge drug discovery methods to identify small
molecule inhibitors of the lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) subtype 5 (LPAR5) receptor is proposed.
Activation of the LPAR5 subtype, blocks antitumor immunity by inhibiting activation of tumor killing
by cytotoxic T lymphocytes, critical for eliminating cancer cells. Small molecule inhibitors of the
LPAR5 receptor should cause a reversal of the inhibition of cytotoxic T cell activation and re-
energize the anti-tumor immune response to treat immune-resistant cancer. Hit compounds
identified in preliminary studies support this hypothesis and form solid premise for the project.

title: Training in noncommunicable diseases epidemiological, data science and Implementation Science research to strengthen evidence-based interventions, policy and control in Uganda.
text: This program is highly relevant to public health because it tackles the escalating global crisis of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and lung health, which are leading drivers of death and disability in the United States. By leveraging Uganda’s unique demographic profiles and healthcare delivery contexts, this initiative expands capacity in advanced data and implementation sciences to generate novel medical insights that cannot be discovered within the US alone. This collaborative training framework builds vital research connections that allow US investigators to co-develop scalable, low-cost clinical interventions, directly accelerating the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of NCDs and reducing severe health challenges across American communities.

title: RADIANT
text: Discovery and Analysis Project Project Summary Diabetes is traditionally classified in two broad categories: autoimmune Type 1 and obesity-related Type 2. Numerous phenotypically and etiologically distinct forms exist and are emerging, collectively termed “atypical diabetes”, that do not fit into either category. We hypothesize that atypical diabetes comprises a spectrum that includes numerous forms, both known (e.g., MODY/monogenic, Ketosis-Prone Diabetes) and unknown. During the current U54 funding cycle we established the Rare and Atypical Diabetes Network (RADIANT), with a well-functioning infrastructure to identify and enroll participants with atypical diabetes; a pipeline for harmonized screening and adjudication of enrolled participants; full genomic characterization of participants via whole genome sequencing; transcriptomic characterization via RNA sequencing; quantitative plasma metabolomics; patient-specific, inducible pluripotent stem cell-based molecular physiology; enrollment of informative family members; and both standard and specialized phenotyping for each participant. In the next cycle of RADIANT, we propose to continue to recruit persons with atypical forms of diabetes to fulfill the original goals, together with discovery and analysis of the mechanisms and pathways that define these new forms of diabetes, by achieving the following Aims: 1) Continue the identification, genome sequencing, transcriptomic and metabolomic interrogation, and deep phenotyping of individuals and families with atypical forms of diabetes; 2) Discover and describe new forms of monogenic diabetes; 3) Expand and enrich the growing database to characterize atypical diabetes and recognize different genotypic and phenotypic clusters; and 4) Determine the pathophysiological mechanisms of atypical diabetes genomic variants. Thus, in the next cycle of RADIANT, our collaborative, multidisciplinary and diverse group of accomplished diabetes investigators will expand our repository of atypical diabetes cases, identify new disease mechanisms, target pathogenic pathways, advance our understanding of diabetes pathophysiology and develop an improved, etiologically based classification of diabetes.

title: Monoclonal Antibody-Conjugated Nanoparticles for Precision CMV Antiviral Deliver
text:
Human cytomegalovirus infection represents a serious health risk, particularly for immunocompromised
individuals and developing fetuses. While existing antiviral therapies have significantly improved clinical
outcomes, their use is often limited by substantial toxicity and off-target effects. Antibody-guided delivery of
nanoparticle-encapsulated antiviral agents offers a promising strategy to enhance therapeutic precision while
minimizing systemic cytotoxicity and associated complications.

title: Exploring the impact of ACSL1’s “BH3-like domain” interaction with MCL-1 on lipid metabolism.
text:
We propose that the cell death machinery and regulation of lipid metabolism are mechanistically linked through
the interaction of the pro-survival protein, MCL-1, and long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase, ACSL1. This proposal
is relevant to the goals of the National Institutes of Health because it identifies how this crosstalk occurs in
models of normal cell biology and mouse physiology.
